In today's episode of the Daily Space Podcast by Flarient, host Ollie dives into an exciting day of space operations and cosmic events. We start with breaking news from orbit: a live test of a wireless power transfer prototype between two spacecraft. This technology could redefine space operations, allowing satellites to share power and dramatically extend their mission lifespans. We break down the engineering behind this milestone, its challenges, and how stable space weather is assisting today's maneuvers.
Next, we shift our focus to planetary defense as near-Earth asteroid 2025 UK9 makes its closest approach to Earth today. We discuss how NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies (CNEOS) tracks these minor planets and why maintaining precise orbital catalogs is crucial for safeguarding our planet.
For skywatchers, we preview the peak of the Draconids meteor shower, offering tips on where to look in the constellation Draco and when to observe after midnight. In our science segments, we explore the official classification of asteroids as minor planets, the physical mechanisms behind sunspots, and how Earth's magnetosphere interacts with solar particles to paint the skies with auroras.
We also cover today's space weather data, featuring a calm Kp index of 1.67, a solar wind speed of 358.2 km/s, and a Dst index of -17 nT. Finally, we look back in history to October 9th of 2017, 2011, and 2005 to remember some of the most powerful solar storms of past solar cycles. Check out live data at flarient.com.

item.title: Asteroid 2026 TP6 Flies By as Orionid Meteors Peak Tonight
item.description:
Welcome to today's edition of the Daily Space Podcast by Flarient for Wednesday, October 14, 2026. Join your host Ollie as we explore a packed day across the solar system and our immediate orbital environment.
Today, we lead with the close approach of near-Earth asteroid 2026 TP6, tracking how orbital observers and radar monitor this rocky visitor as it safely glides past. Simultaneously, Earth plunges into the ancient debris stream left behind by Comet 1P/Halley, producing the peak of the Orionids meteor shower with up to twenty swift meteors per hour lighting up dark skies.
In our space weather report, we analyse live telemetry from NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center and the GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences. With the planetary Kp index hovering quietly between 0.67 and 2.33, the headline story remains an invisible one: a high-speed solar wind stream surging at 611.7 km/s from an open coronal hole, held at bay only by a northward-pointing interplanetary magnetic field (Bz at +2.5 nT). We look back at the dramatic G3 strong geomagnetic storm that rocked Earth's magnetosphere on October 10th with an 852 km/s blast, and look ahead on the watch calendar to Jupiter reaching opposition on January 10, 2027.
We also examine new insights into astrobiology and extreme planetary habitability, compare atmospheric evolution on Earth and Mars, and dive into the technological realities of asteroid mining—from volatile extraction to orbital refuelling depots. Finally, we tackle a persistent myth regarding polar mesospheric clouds and verify the real-world science behind noctilucent cloud formation.

item.description:

In this episode, host Ollie breaks down the aftermath of the significant G3 geomagnetic storm that struck on October 10th and tracks the latest telemetry as our magnetosphere transitions into a much-needed period of quiet recovery.
We lead with breaking tracking updates on near-Earth asteroid 2026 TP6, which is executing a close flyby past Earth today. We examine how planetary defence teams use these encounters to refine orbital models, and look ahead to the celestial fireworks of the approaching Orionids meteor shower peaking on October 22nd.

item.description:

item.title: [WEEKLY] Asteroid 2025 UK9 Flyby, Orionids Peak, and Solar Calm
item.description:
Welcome to the Sunday Weekly Roundup on the Daily Space Podcast by Flarient for October 18, 2026. In this comprehensive review of our local space environment, host Ollie examines a fascinating cosmic double feature happening right above our heads. Near-Earth asteroid 2025 UK9 makes its closest approach to our planet, coinciding with the annual peak of the Orionids meteor shower—a stream of ancient debris shed by Comet 1P/Halley hitting our upper atmosphere at blistering speeds with zenithal hourly rates reaching twenty meteors per hour.
Alongside these astronomical spectacles, our star has settled into a remarkably peaceful state. We dive into the live space weather metrics from NOAA and the Space Weather Prediction Center, analyzing a quiet Kp index of 0.67, a benign interplanetary magnetic field with Bz hovering around positive 3.2 nT, and solar wind speeds clocking in at 423.4 kilometres per second. Ollie explores what these tranquil conditions mean for satellite drag, high-frequency communications, and global navigation systems, as well as auroral visibility confined strictly to high polar latitudes.
We also explore the week's foundational space weather science, unpacking our latest deep-dive articles. We untangle the vital physical distinctions between instantaneous electromagnetic solar flares travelling at the speed of light and massive coronal mass ejections (CMEs) that propel billions of tonnes of plasma across the solar system over days. Plus, we explore how differential solar rotation winds up internal magnetic fields to generate sunspots, and how charged solar wind particles ignite the glowing red, green, and purple curtains of the aurora borealis.
